_comment: ANY.RUN for BinaryPivot. The ANY.RUN API is, in practice, a SANDBOX-SUBMISSION API: you send it a file or a URL, it detonates it in an interactive VM and gives you back a task with the network log, dropped files and a verdict. Threat Intelligence Lookup (searching other people's detonations without running your own) is a SEPARATE and comparatively LIMITED product — a distinct licence, a small request allowance, and absent entirely from a plain sandbox subscription — so treat TI Lookup as a bonus when the licence happens to exist, and the sandbox as the layer's real surface. That surface has an OPSEC cost the static tooling does not: submitting is an OUTBOUND, ATTRIBUTABLE, OFTEN-PUBLIC act performed against live case infrastructure, which is why `submission_policy` below requires the ANALYST'S EXPLICIT CONFIRMATION every time and the code refuses without it. This file holds everything about ANY.RUN that changes without our code changing: API paths, submission options and their privacy semantics, the TI Lookup query grammar, the pivot-kind map, the entitlement matrix, the request guard and the web-UI links the KEYLESS path emits. Edit this file, not bp_anyrun.py. Nothing here is case data — public product facts only.

endpoints._comment: ANY.RUN REST paths. `api_base` is the v1 API root, `report_base` serves the per-task report renderings, `content_base` the downloadable artifacts. Auth is `Authorization: API-KEY <key>` on every call (the client adds the prefix if you paste a bare key). `submit_analysis` is a POST — `obj_type=file` as multipart, `obj_type=url` as form fields — and is the ONE endpoint here that changes the world outside this machine: it is gated by `submission_policy`, never called without explicit confirmation, and never called automatically by a collector. Everything else is read-only. `stop_task` / `delete_task` exist so a submission made in error can be pulled quickly — deletion removes it from YOUR history, it does not un-see anything the target already observed.

privacy_types._comment: `opt_privacy_type` on a submission — who can see the resulting task. This is the single most consequential option on the whole API and the SDK's own default (`bylink`) is NOT the safe one for investigative work. `public` puts the sample, the URL, the screenshots and the full network log into a feed that anyone — including the operator — can search; ANY.RUN's public feed is routinely monitored by the people who build these funnels. `owner` is the default this tool uses. On a FREE plan the private options are not available at all, which is precisely why a free-plan submission must be refused rather than quietly downgraded.

entries.owner: only you — the default this tool submits with, and the only one that is safe by construction
entries.byteam: your team — acceptable when the whole team is on the engagement
entries.bylink: anyone holding the URL: not indexed, but forwardable and guessable-adjacent; the SDK's default, NOT ours
entries.public: EVERYONE, in a searchable feed the operator can watch. Refused by this tool unless explicitly forced

submission_policy._comment: THE CONFIRMATION GATE. A submission is not a lookup: it takes the analyst's case material and hands it to a third party, then reaches out and TOUCHES the target from a fingerprintable sandbox. Both halves can burn an investigation, and neither is reversible — deleting the task afterwards does not un-send the sample and does not un-notify the operator. So the rule is absolute: the code NEVER submits without the analyst saying yes to THIS submission, and the model must put the risks in front of the user and ask, not infer consent from 'analyze this sample'. `preflight_checks` is what to try FIRST — most triage questions are answered without detonating anything at all. `never_send` is RULE 1 crossing an API boundary: case identifiers must not travel in `user_tags` or a filename.
risks: PUBLIC EXPOSURE — on a free/public plan every submission is world-readable and searchable: the sample, the URL, the screenshots and the network log. Operators monitor the public feed for their own domains and hashes

TIPPING THE OPERATOR — a URL detonation FETCHES the live target. ANY.RUN's egress ranges are published, so the operator sees a known sandbox hit their funnel: they rotate the infrastructure, or start serving a decoy, and the case gets harder from that moment on

A POISONED VERDICT — the same filtering means a benign result may simply be the decoy these funnels serve to datacenter IPs. 'info' is not exoneration; without a residential-proxy option you may be grading the operator's cloaking, not their malware
THIRD-PARTY DATA HANDLING — the sample may carry victim PII, client data or material you are not licensed to redistribute. Uploading it is a disclosure decision, and it may be a legal one
ATTRIBUTION AND TIMING — a submission is a timestamped act tied to your account, and it places your interest in this target on someone else's record
preflight_checks: Run the static analysis first — analyze_artifact usually answers the triage question with zero outbound contact
Look for an EXISTING detonation before creating one: the file hash on TI Lookup (if licensed), VirusTotal, MalwareBazaar, Triage, Koodous, or a public ANY.RUN task. Somebody has often already run it
If it must be detonated, confirm the privacy setting is `owner`/`byteam` — never `public`

For a URL, remember the target LEARNS it was sandboxed. Decide whether that is acceptable at this stage of the case, and prefer detonating the downloaded FILE over the live URL where that answers the question
Strip case identifiers from filenames and tags before sending anything
never_send: case IDs or case-folder names in user_tags, filenames or any submitted metadata
the analyst's or the client's name
any sample containing victim PII that is not necessary to the question being asked

query_fields._comment: The TI Lookup query grammar. A query is one or more `field:"value"` terms joined with AND/OR; the API takes it as the `query` field of the search body, and the same string is what you paste into the TI Lookup web UI. Listed here so the tool can name the RIGHT field for an artifact instead of guessing — `destinationIP` and `domainName` are network-observation fields, so a hit means a sandboxed sample actually contacted that host, which is a much stronger statement than a string appearing in a binary. Add a field when ANY.RUN adds one; the value is what appears after the colon.

entries.sha256: file hash of a submitted or dropped sample
entries.destinationPort: the port of that connection — pair with destinationIP for a C2 endpoint
entries.url: a full URL requested during detonation
entries.threatName: the family/threat label ANY.RUN assigned (e.g. a stealer or RAT name)
entries.filePath: a path the sample wrote to
entries.fileEventPath: a path involved in a file event
entries.imagePath: the executable image path of a spawned process
entries.commandLine: the command line of a spawned process
entries.suricataID: the Suricata signature ID that fired
entries.ja3: client TLS fingerprint of the sample's own traffic
entries.ja3s: server TLS fingerprint seen in that traffic
entries.jarm: JARM of the contacted server — joins straight onto WebPivot's own jarm:hash pivot
entries.submissionCountry: country the task was submitted from

pivot_field_map._comment: BinaryPivot pivot `kind` -> the TI Lookup field that reverses it. `file:sha256`, `app:backend_host` and `app:c2_endpoint` are the kinds analyze_artifact actually emits; `file:md5` / `file:sha1` are the CLI's own hash flags; `domain` / `ip` / `url` / `jarm:hash` are the WebPivot-shaped kinds, since a BinaryPivot result is ingested through the same schema. A kind that is absent gets no ANY.RUN query, which is correct for artifacts the sandbox does not index — an APK package name, a signing certificate and a firebase project id are identity, not observation, and belong on VirusTotal/Koodous/Triage instead. `app:c2_endpoint` is special-cased in code: an `ip:port` value is split into destinationIP + destinationPort so the query matches the CONNECTION rather than a literal string that appears in no index. Prefix entries ending in `:` match any kind starting with that prefix.

verdict_levels._comment: How to read the threat level on a returned task, so a report says what was OBSERVED rather than repeating a vendor label. `info` on a live scam host is not exoneration — an interactive sandbox that was served a benign decoy (geo/UA/referrer filtering is standard on these funnels) records exactly that.

entries.malicious: the sandbox scored the behaviour as malicious
entries.info: nothing malicious observed in THAT detonation — check whether the sample was served a decoy

plan_capabilities._comment: What each ANY.RUN entitlement allows, so the tool degrades with an accurate sentence instead of an opaque 401/403. The important asymmetry: MOST keys are sandbox keys. TI Lookup is a separate, comparatively limited licence with its own small allowance, and a sandbox subscription does NOT include it — so `ti_lookup` and `sandbox_api` are tracked apart and the tool checks rather than assumes. `private_submission` records whether the plan can submit anything other than PUBLIC: on the free tier it cannot, and a submission there would expose the sample to a feed the operator can read, which is why the policy refuses instead of downgrading.

none.note: no key — the query BUILDER and the UI links still work; nothing is queried or submitted from here

free.note: FREE community plan: every submission is PUBLIC and searchable. Fine for reading other people's public tasks, unacceptable for submitting live case infrastructure — the policy refuses

sandbox.note: paid sandbox key: submit with owner/byteam privacy, plus task history and reports for YOUR OWN submissions; /intelligence/* still answers 401/403

ti_trial.note: TI Lookup trial: a small fixed request allowance — spend it on the two or three artifacts that actually decide the case

ti_full.note: full TI Lookup licence: lookup + YARA search + feeds, alongside the sandbox

request_budget._comment: THE SPEND GUARD. A TI Lookup trial is measured in tens of requests, not thousands, and the failure mode is the usual one — the allowance runs out mid-batch and the empty answers read as 'this sample is unknown to the sandbox world'. So requests are counted from MEMORY/api_usage.jsonl before the call and capped per run and per month, the same pattern as the Censys and IntelX guards. Override per run with ANYRUN_MAX_REQUESTS_PER_RUN / ANYRUN_MONTHLY_REQUESTS.

result_limits._comment: Per-call ceilings so one lookup cannot dominate a case file. `max_tasks` bounds the related sandbox tasks kept per artifact; `lookup_days` is the default time window (ANY.RUN expects an explicit start/end date, and an unbounded window is both slower and noisier).

ui_templates._comment: The KEYLESS deliverable. ANY.RUN's TI Lookup UI does not take a shareable query URL, so the emitted entry is the UI address PLUS the exact query text to paste — building the right query is most of the skill, and that part costs nothing. `public_task` opens one public sandbox session by uuid; `submissions` is the public feed. Keep these as data: ANY.RUN moves UI paths independently of its API.

clustering_policy._comment: FALSE-POSITIVE CONTROL — read this before turning an ANY.RUN hit into a same-operator edge. A sandbox observation says a sample CONTACTED a host; it does not say who owns it. Half of what a detonation contacts is shared internet furniture, and a threat-family label groups by KIT, not by operator — two crews running the same commodity stealer are not one crew. `cluster_on` is what may support an edge (an operator-specific host or C2 endpoint reached by a sample you already tie to the case); `context_only` is everything that describes the malware family or the environment. Same rule as everywhere else in this repo: corroborate with a second, independent artifact class before committing.
clustering_policy.note: A shared threatName is a same-KIT signal, exactly like a shared app protector or a shared white-label CDN — record it as kit-level and do not let it carry an attribution claim on its own.
